list-item.p: An LDC regimen achieves CR rates noninferior to standard-dose therapy, with comparable 4-year EFS, OS, and cumulative incidence of relapse.
The LDC regimen reduces durations of neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, and lowers remission induction costs.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Intensive chemotherapy is standard for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) but carries high risks of life-threatening complications, particularly in vulnerable patients. We aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of a low-dose chemotherapy (LDC) regimen for induction of AML. A randomized, multicenter, noninferiority trial was conducted in patients with AML aged <18 years. Patients received low-dose cytarabine, mitoxantrone or idarubicin, and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) or standard-dose chemotherapy (SDC; cytarabine, daunomycin, and etoposide). All patients received postremission consolidation with standard chemotherapy and/or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The primary end point was to compare response rates between treatments. The secondary end points were to compare the outcomes, toxicity, and safety of the LDC and SDC regimens. The 2 treatment arms showed no significant differences in outcomes. Complete remission (CR)/CR with incomplete count recovery rates after induction were 95.1% and 95.3% in the LDC and SDC arms, respectively. Measurable residual disease <0.1% after induction II was observed in 87.4% and 87.1% of patients in the LDC and SDC arms, respectively. Median time to neutrophil and platelet recovery was significantly shorter among patients receiving the LDC regimen. Patients in the LDC arm had a 4-year overall survival (OS) of 81.3% vs 83.6% (P = .611), and a 4-year event-free survival (EFS) of 61.5% vs 63.1% (P = .832). In conclusion, the LDC regimen was well tolerated, and was associated with CR, EFS, and OS rates that were not inferior to those of patients treated with the SDC regimen. The trial was registered at www.chictr.org.cn as ChiCTR1800015883.

Induction therapy for pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is highly intensive and carries significant risks of toxicity. Gao and colleagues report results from the phase 3 CALS III-AML18 trial, showing that low-dose induction chemotherapy with granulocyte colony-stimulating factor achieves remission rates and survival outcomes comparable to those with standard-dose induction therapy in children with AML. This low-dose regimen is associated with fewer toxicities, faster hematologic recovery, and reduced health care costs, suggesting a feasible treatment strategy for resource-limited settings. Further validation of this chemotherapy deescalation regimen is needed for optimization of low-dose approaches.

sec.p: Received 2025 Jul 23; Accepted 2026 Feb 13; Issue date 2026 Jul 2.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a rare, heterogeneous, malignant disorder of the hematopoietic stem cells.1 Overall survival (OS) rates for pediatric AML increased dramatically as a result of the introduction of intensive chemotherapy regimens, improved supportive care, reproducible AML risk classification, and access to allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).2, 3, 4 In high-income countries, OS rates for children with AML have varied between 70% and 80%.5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 Attempts to intensify remission-induction chemotherapy further have not improved outcomes and have raised concerns about the acute and long-term complications.14,15 Moreover, intensive chemotherapy has been associated with high early-treatment mortality rates in low- and middle-income countries because of deficiencies in the available supportive care, including limitations on access to blood products and antimicrobial drugs.16,17 Effective drugs have been approved for treating AML, especially in adults.18 Integrating these new agents into the current AML regimens, which are already highly myelosuppressive, is a significant obstacle to determining their efficacy and toxicity.

In 2012, to improve access to AML treatment, we implemented a reduced-intensity remission-induction chemotherapy approach.19 This pilot study aimed to treat newly diagnosed pediatric patients with AML with severe infections or at high-risk treatment abandonment using low-intensity chemotherapy (LDC) regimens, a strategy commonly used for older patients with AML in Asia.20, 21, 22 A retrospective nonrandomized analysis of 83 children treated with LDC at our institution showed outcomes comparable to those receiving standard regimens.19,23 Here, we present findings from a prospective, randomized, multicentric trial confirming the noninferiority of the LDC regimen.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Previously untreated patients aged <18 years with newly diagnosed AML were enrolled on the CALS III-AML18 protocol at 11 medical centers in China. Details on the statistical analysis are available in the supplemental Appendix 2 (available on the Blood website). The protocol was approved by the medical ethics committee of the Children’s Hospital of Soochow University (number 2017047-1) and was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registration Center (chictr.org.cn identifier: ChiCTR1800015883). Informed consent was obtained from all patients or their legal guardians in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Response criteria
sec.p: We used the 2017 European LeukemiaNet (ELN) recommendations24 to standardize assessment of morphologic and cytogenetic features at diagnosis and response evaluation. Morphologic complete remission (CR) was defined as <5% bone marrow blasts (absence of cells with Auer rods, or extramedullary leukemia) with hematologic recovery (transfusion-free, absolute neutrophil count of >1.0 × 109/L and platelet count of >80.0 × 109/L). CR with incomplete count recovery (CRi) met the CR morphologic criteria without full hematologic recovery. Partial response required ≥50% decrease in bone marrow blasts, leaving 5% to 19% blasts. Nonresponders had ≥20% blasts. Bone marrow was evaluated on day 26 of induction I and II. Patients in CR/CRi received subsequent chemotherapy courses (induction II or consolidation I) by day 36. Measurable residual disease (MRD), assessed by flow cytometry, was considered positive at ≥0.1% after induction II and incorporated into risk classification using a pediatric-specific model (supplemental Methods).

sec.title: Study design and treatment
sec.p: Patients diagnosed with AML were randomized to receive either LDC or standard-dose chemotherapy (SDC) induction therapy using a stratified block randomization method25 (block size = 4). Stratification factors include the treating hospital, age at initial diagnosis (<10 or ≥10 years), white blood cell (WBC) count (<25 × 109/L or ≥25 × 109/L), and initial use of prophase cytoreductive cytarabine (yes or no). Patients who were medically unfit for standard therapy or judged to be at high risk for treatment abandonment received the lower-intensity regimen off protocol. Their data were intentionally excluded from the randomized trial analysis. Patients who presented with a WBC count >50 × 109/L received cytoreductive cytarabine therapy as a prophase for up to 5 days. Those whose counts remained above this threshold after cytoreduction were not randomized. Inclusion and exclusion criteria as well as the indications for HSCT are detailed in the supplemental Methods. Patients received 2 remission-induction courses of either LDC (cytarabine 10 mg/m2, subcutaneous, every 12 hours, 20 doses; mitoxantrone or idarubicin 5 mg/m2, IV, days 1, 3, and 5; and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor [G-CSF] 5 μg/kg, subcutaneous, daily, 10 doses) or SDC (cytarabine 100 mg/m2, IV, every 12 hours, 20 doses; daunorubicin 50 mg/m2, IV, days 1, 3, and 5; and etoposide 100 mg2, IV, days 1-5). Patients in CR received 2 to 3 cycles of intensive consolidation chemotherapy and/or underwent HSCT based on relapse risk. A fourth consolidation course (fludarabine, cytarabine, and G-CSF) was recommended for patients eligible for HSCT who were unable to proceed with transplant (supplemental Table 1). The cumulative doses of chemotherapeutic agents administered on each arm, along with comparisons to published studies, are presented in supplemental Methods.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The first of the study’s 2 primary objectives was to determine whether the experimental LDC regimen was noninferior to the SDC regimen in achieving CR/CRi, using a noninferiority margin of ≤0.05. The end point is “induction success,” defined by achieving CR/CRi at the end of induction I or induction II. According to the prespecified statistical design, a 1-sided 70% upper confidence bound to the difference in induction success probability (SDC − LDC) was calculated. The LDC regimen was considered noninferior if this upper confidence bound was ≤0.05. The noninferiority margin of 0.05 was selected based on preliminary data indicating that the CR/CRi rate in childhood AML is ∼88% (0.88). Therefore, a decrease in induction success probability of ≤0.05 was considered clinically acceptable for the LDC arm. We adopted the 70% upper confidence bound to balance statistical accuracy (control of false-positive probability) with efficiency (adequate power within a feasible sample size; see protocol and supplemental Table 3).

Sample size and power were evaluated over a range of plausible induction success probabilities derived from previous studies: 0.85 to 0.95 for SDC and 0.75 to 0.95 for LDC (supplemental Table 3). A total of 300 evaluable patients (150 per arm) provided ∼80% power to demonstrate noninferiority when the induction success probabilities were equal between treatment groups, while ensuring that the false-positive probability (ie, declaring noninferiority when the true difference >0.05) decreases rapidly to ≈0.2 or less (supplemental Table 3). To account for the possibility that up to 25% of randomized patients might be unevaluable for the primary end point, the target accrual was set at 400 patients. Ultimately, 438 eligible patients were randomized. A post hoc analysis was conducted to calculate the 95% upper confidence bound for the difference in CR/CRi probability after each remission induction to supplement the noninferiority finding.

The second primary objective was to compare remission-induction treatment costs between the 2 groups. Depending on the distribution of the cost data, differences were evaluated using a 2-sample t test or Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and results were reported with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Treatment costs were estimated from billing charges associated with inpatient admissions and outpatient encounters. The overall cost of induction I and induction II included charges for blood products, antibiotics, and other supportive care, as well as expenses incurred during intensive care unit admissions and consultation by other subspecialties. Detailed charge data were obtained directly from hospital cost centers.

In analyses of secondary objectives, including outcomes and toxicity, OS and event-free survival (EFS) were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, with comparisons made via the log-rank test. Four-year OS and EFS estimates were reported with log-log 95% CIs. EFS was defined as the time from diagnosis until death, refractory disease, or relapse of any type, whichever occurred first. OS was calculated from the time of diagnosis to death from any cause. Time was censored at the date of last patient contact if no event occurred. The cumulative incidence of relapse and refractory disease (CIR) was estimated using the Kalbfleisch-Prentice method, and comparisons between groups were performed using Gray test. The time origin for all CIR analyses was the date of diagnosis. For the CIR end point, failure events included no remission after induction I or II and partial remission after induction II; the date of failure was defined as the date these determinations were made. Death or withdrawal from study before a failure event was treated as a competing risk. The follow-up time was summarized for patients who remained event-free at their last contact. Quartiles of follow-up time, corresponding to OS follow-up, were estimated using the reverse Kaplan-Meier method.

Adverse events (AEs) were graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.0, with AEs of grade ≥3 classified as severe. The probabilities of severe AEs were compared between the 2 randomized groups using the χ22 test for contingency tables.
Per study design, randomized patients who completed induction I were considered evaluable. All randomized and evaluable patients were included and analyzed according to modified intent to treat.
All P values were 2-sided, with a significance threshold defined as .05. Data were current as of 31 January 2025.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: From June 2018 to October 2021, 438 of 484 patients with newly diagnosed AML were randomized to receive an LDC regimen (n = 223) or an SDC regimen (n = 215). Thirty-seven patients were excluded from randomization and analysis due to randomization refusal. An additional 9 patients with cytarabine-refractory hyperleukocytosis (WBC count of >50 × 109/L after 5 days of cytarabine) received the SDC regimen and were not randomized. Of the 83 patients who presented with a WBC count of >50 × 109/L at diagnosis and responded to the cytarabine prophase, 40 were treated in the LDC arm and 43 in the SDC arm. There was no significant difference in the use of cytarabine between the 2 groups (P = .712).

After randomization but before initiation of chemotherapy, 38 patients were excluded from the study for the following reasons: withdrawal of consent by families or patients (n = 15; 11 abandonments, 4 withdrawals); ineligibility due to diagnostic misclassification as non-de novo AML (n = 19); and pretreatment death (n = 4). As a result, 400 of 438 randomized patients proceeded to receive therapy, 200 assigned to LDC and 200 to SDC, and were included in the final analysis (Figure 1). Among the patients who were event-free at the last follow-up, the median follow-up time of the study was 55.1 months (interquartile range, 43.7-65.4). Over a median follow-up period of 28.8 months, 17 patients (4.3%) were lost to follow-up, and 10 (2.5%) abandoned treatment. No patients with second myeloid neoplasms have been reported in the study cohort.

sec.title: Clinical and biological characteristics
sec.p: Baseline clinical and laboratory characteristics did not differ significantly between the 2 arms (Table 1). The median age was 7.2 years (interquartile range, 3.8-10.7). Cytogenetic analysis, including fluorescence in situ hybridization, was successful in 388 patients (97.0%). Two hundred seventy-four patients (68.5%) had one of the World Health Organization class–defining AML recurrent rearrangements.26 Normal and complex karyotypes were found in 99 patients (25.5%) and 23 patients (5.9%), respectively. Genomic studies, including deep sequencing and whole-transcriptome sequencing analysis, were performed in 354 patients (88.5%) and 217 patients (54.3%), respectively. Twenty-two patients were analyzed with a targeted genetic panel that included 43 gene fusions and mutations. Core-binding factor AML (CBF-AML) accounted for 41.8% of this cohort, KMT2A rearrangements for 21.0%, and NUP98 or NUP214 rearrangements for 5.5%.

sec.p: Among leukemia-associated gene variants, CEBPA (CCAAT enhancer-binding protein α) double mutations, KIT (KIT proto-oncogene, receptor tyrosine kinase) mutations, and FLT3-ITD (FMS-like tyrosine kinase 3 gene internal tandem duplication) abnormalities were identified in 9.8%, 23.0%, and 11.8% of patients, respectively. Detailed mutational landscapes are provided in supplemental Figure 1A. Of the 340 patients who achieved CR, 160 (47.1%) underwent HSCT.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Induction success (CR/CRi after induction I or II) was achieved in 168 of 200 (84.0%) patients in LDC, and 172 of 200 (86.0%) in SDC. The 70% upper confidence bound for the difference (SDC − LDC) was 0.039, meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion for the LDC regimen in achieving remission. After induction I, CR/CRi was attained in 143 of 200 (71.5%) patients in the LDC group and 140 of 200 (70.0%) in the SDC group (P = .742); the 95% upper confidence bound for the difference (SDC − LDC) was 0.060. After induction II, CR/CRi was attained in 156 of 168 (95.1%) recipients of LDC,and 164 of 172 (95.3%) recipients of SDC (P = .922), with a 95% upper confidence bound for the difference (SDC − LDC) of 0.041 (Table 2). After induction I, MRD <1% was observed in 66.2% of patients receiving LDC, and in 71.4% of those receiving SDC (P = .260). Using the stricter threshold of MRD (<0.1%), the corresponding rates were 56.9% in the LDC group, and 64.3% in the SDC group (P = .136). Following induction II, MRD <0.1% was observed in 87.4% of patients who received LDC and 87.1% of patients who received SDC (P = .922; supplemental Table 4). The 2 treatment arms were also comparable with respect to CR or CRi status after induction I or induction II (supplemental Table 5), and the proportion of patients who initiated a second induction course on day 26 (supplemental Table 6).

Nonresponders after induction I were taken off of the protocol.

sec.p: Subgroup analyses of MRD negativity after induction I revealed statistically significant differences favoring SDC in specific populations at the 2-sided 5% level. In patients with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 rearrangement or KIT mutations or ELN-2022 favorable risk group, the MRD negativity rates after induction I were significantly lower in the LDC group than in the SDC group (P = .001, P = .011, and P = .009, respectively). However, when compared with patients treated with SDC, LDC did not confer a MRD negativity advantage in any specific AML subgroup (Figure 2). As for CR rates after induction I, in patients with NUP rearrangement, CR was 64.3% (95% CI, 38.8-83.7) for LDC compared with 0% (95% CI, 0-32.4) for SDC (P = .006). In patients with FLT3-ITD, CR was 70.8% (95% CI, 50.8-85.1) for LDC compared with 39.1% (95% CI, 22.2-59.2) for SDC (P = .042). Conversely, in patients with KIT mutations, CR rates were 70.0% (95% CI, 54.6-81.9) for LDC, and 88.5% (95% CI, 77.0-94.6) for SDC (P = .035; supplemental Figure 2).

sec.p: The association between specific genetic mutations and induction I treatment response I is illustrated in supplemental Figure 1B. No significant differences were observed in the biological characteristics of nonresponders between the 2 groups after induction I (supplemental Table 7). No significant differences in MRD negativity rates were observed between the 2 groups after induction II (supplemental Table 8; supplemental Figure 3).

sec.title: AEs and treatment costs
sec.p: All 400 patients were included in the safety analysis for induction therapy. The main toxicities during inductions I and II are summarized in Tables 3 and 4. Remission induction was well tolerated in both arms, with significantly fewer grade ≥3 toxicities in the LDC arm. In induction I, nausea or vomiting occurred in 0.0% of recipients of LDC and 11.0% of recipients of SDC (P < .001), colitis in 2.5% vs 9.5% (P = .003), and bleeding in 0% vs 3.0% (P = .030) (Table 3). In induction II, febrile neutropenia occurred in 25.6% of recipients of LDC and 50.0% of recipients of SDC (P < .001), lung or sinus infection in 9.5% vs 19.2% (P = .010), and sepsis in 4.2% vs 11.6% (P = .012) (Table 4).

sec.p: The incidence of hematologic AEs (grade ≥3) after induction I was similar between LDC and SDC, including neutropenia (89% vs 93%; P = .162), thrombocytopenia (88.5% vs 93.5%; P = .081), and anemia (68.5% vs 70.5%; P = .664). However, the LDC regimen was associated with significantly faster neutrophil and platelet recovery compared with standard therapy. The median time to neutrophil recovery to ≥0.5 × 109/L was 19 vs 22 days in induction I (P < .001) and 12 vs 15 days in induction II (P < .001). The median time to platelet count ≥20.0 × 109/L was 13 vs 17 days in induction I (P < .001) and 3 vs 8 days in induction II (P < .001; Figure 3). Fifteen patients died during remission induction: 4 in the LDC arm and 11 in the SDC arm (2.0% vs 5.5%; P = .065; Table 2). Causes of death included severe infections (n = 13 [86.7%]) and bleeding in vital organs (n = 2 [13.3%]). G-CSF was temporarily held in 8 patients (4.0%) because of a WBC count of ≥50.0 × 109/L, restarted after a median of 2 days (range, 1-3) with no recurrence of leukocytosis. Missed G-CSF doses were not replaced.

caption.p: Comparison of neutrophil and platelet recovery time between the 2 groups. Violin plots illustrate the distribution and the median of neutrophil and platelet recovery time (days) after the first (A,C) and second (B,D) courses of LDC or SDC.

sec.p: The total treatment costs for remission induction I and II, as well as red cell and platelet transfusion requirements, were significantly lower for recipients of LDC (supplemental Figure 4).

sec.title: Survival outcomes
sec.p: Recipients of LDC had a 4-year OS of 81.3% (95% CI, 78.6-89.0), compared with 83.6% (95% CI, 76.0-87.0) for recipients of SDC (P = .611; Figure 4A); a 4-year EFS of 61.5% (95% CI, 54.9-68.9) vs 63.1% (95% CI, 56.7-70.3; P = .832; Figure 4B); and a 4-year CIR of 30.7% (95% CI, 24.2-37.3) vs 25.1% (95% CI, 19.2-31.4; P = .210; Figure 4C). The differences (SDC − LDC) in OS and EFS between groups were 2.3% (95% CI, −5.33 to 9.93) and 1.6% (95% CI, −8.23 to 11.43), respectively, thus no statistically significant differences in OS or EFS. Given the lower MRD negativity rate among patients with CBF-AML harboring KIT mutations in the LDC group, we performed a subgroup survival analysis. In this subgroup, OS was lower in the LDC group, with a trend toward statistical significance (P = .057; supplemental Figure 5A); EFS was also lower in the LDC group (P = .002; supplemental Figure 5B). Additionally, CIR was significantly higher in the LDC group compared with the SDC group (P < .001; supplemental Figure 5C). Conversely, in patients without CBF and KIT mutations, the CIR in the LDC group trended slightly lower (P = .550; supplemental Figure 5D), indicating that the higher overall CIR in the LDC group compared with the SDC group was attributable to a higher relapse rate in patients with CBF-AML with KIT mutations treated by the LDC regimen.

caption.p: Comparison of survival between 2 induction treatment groups. Kaplan-Meier plots of OS (A), EFS (B), and CIR (C) according to the treatment arm.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Previous studies have established the response rates and toxicity of the combination of low-dose cytarabine and anthracycline administered concurrently with G-CSF (LDC) in older patients with relapsed or de novo high-risk myeloid neoplasms.20, 21, 22 A retrospective analysis from our institution demonstrated the feasibility and safety of LDC in children with de novo AML,19 and suggested comparable long-term outcomes to standard-dose cytarabine, anthracycline, and etoposide (SDC) for remission induction.23 However, few randomized controlled trials have been conducted to evaluate its efficacy and safety in comparison with the current standard treatment.

In this study, noninferiority inference was applied to the predefined end point of induction success, defined as achieving CR/CRi at the end of either induction I or II. Using this end point, we demonstrated that the LDC regimen was noninferior to the SDC regimen in inducing remission. This composite end point has been previously used in a randomized childhood AML trial.27 We also evaluated post hoc CR/CRi rates separately after induction I and after induction II, confirming that the treatment-arm differences at each time point were consistent with those observed using the combined induction success end point. Although the MRD negativity rate tended to be lower in the LDC group after induction I, rates were comparable between the 2 groups after induction II. Long-term outcomes, including CR rates, 4-year EFS, 4-year OS, and CIR, were also comparable between the treatment arms, supporting the overall efficacy of the LDC regimen. This study establishes that a low-intensity regimen with concurrent G-CSF is noninferior to a myelosuppressive combination for inducing remission of pediatric AML.

Treatment-related toxicities were less common in the LDC arm, with a significantly shorter duration of neutropenia and thrombocytopenia after induction I and II. Severe nonhematologic toxicities, including lungs, sinuses, and gastrointestinal infections, as well as sepsis, were significantly more frequent in the SDC arm, particularly during induction II. Induction treatment-related deaths, usually due to infection, were higher in SDC recipients, especially during induction I, whereas no deaths occurred during induction II in the LDC arm. The rates of treatment-related mortality during induction of 3.75% for all study enrollees and 2.0% in the LDC arm compare favorably with those described in multicenter pediatric AML clinical trials.4,8,10, 11, 12

Starting G-CSF on day 1 of induction I (in the LDC arm) was safe. To reduce leukocytosis and leukostasis risks, cytarabine alone (100 mg/m2, every 12 hours, 2-5 days) was administered for patients with WBC counts of ≥50.0 × 109/L, and LDC induction started when the WBC counts decreased below that level. In rare instances when the WBC count increased during the first few days of chemotherapy, G-CSF was temporarily stopped, and restarted when the WBC counts decreased below 50.0 × 109/L. We observed no uncontrolled leukocytosis or clinical manifestations of leukostasis.

Despite their typical association with high-risk disease,28, 29, 30 patients with NUP-rearranged AML achieved markedly higher CR rates with LDC (9/14 [64.3%]) than with SDC (0/8 [0%]). Similarly, patients with FLT3-ITD mutations showed higher response rates with LDC, although confirmation will require larger cohorts. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, but warrant further investigation in prospective studies focused on these molecular AML subgroups.

Conversely, patients with KIT mutations, usually co-occurring with CBF-AML, had significantly worse CR when treated with the LDC regimen. Only 54.1% of patients with AML with KIT mutations treated with the LDC regimen attained MRD remission <0.1%, compared with 80.4% of SDC recipients. KIT mutations frequently co-occur with CBF-AML and, in our study, patients with CBF-AML harboring KIT mutations had inferior survival outcomes when treated with the LDC regimen. A recent study showed that patients with CBF-AML with exon 17 KIT mutations and MRD ≥0.1% at the end of induction had dismal 5-year EFS even after intensive chemotherapy approaches.31 We do not recommend the LDC regimen for CBF-AML with KIT mutations based on our study and reported data. A small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor specifically designed to target KIT and PDDGFRa activation loop mutations has been approved for gastrointestinal stromal tumors. Whether selective KIT inhibitors will affect the outcome of pediatric CBF-AML with KIT mutations remains to be seen.32

In this study, the LDC regimen demonstrated notable efficacy in the ELN high-risk subgroup, achieving a CR rate of 72.0%, and MRD negativity of 62.0% after induction I. These results suggest an opportunity to enhance the LDC platform by integrating small-molecule inhibitors, such as menin inhibitors for KMT2A rearranged or NUP98 rearranged AML, and FLT3-ITD inhibitors for FLT3-ITD+ disease.33, 34, 35 Such combinations have the potential to enhance outcomes while maintaining LDC’s reduced toxicity profile. Future studies should evaluate this strategy in prospective trials focused on adverse risk pediatric cohorts.

Our study has also broad implications for clinical management and investigation of pediatric AML. In regions with limited resources and high mortality rates for AML induction chemotherapy, the LDC regimen offers an alternative approach to increase remission rates by reducing treatment-related mortality. However, adequate supportive care is required to deliver intensive postremission approaches, including HSCT, to improve OS in these settings. The study has several limitations, including the sample size, which did not allow for a definitive conclusion about predictive risk factors associated with the treatment arms. Extending the number of patients in each treatment arm would allow for clarifying the impact of AML-associated variables on outcomes. Similarly, although the CIR did not differ significantly between the 2 treatment arms, a larger cohort may reveal a higher relapse rate in the LDC arm. A nonsignificant trend toward increased HSCT use was observed among patients assigned to the LDC arm, raising the possibility that reduced induction chemotherapy intensity could expand the pool of transplant candidates. However, the trial was not powered or designed to assess the impact of postremission treatment strategies; therefore, no definitive conclusions can be drawn.

In conclusion, in this randomized trial, children with AML treated with a low-intensity regimen, G-CSF–supported induction regimen achieved noninferior remission rates and comparable long-term outcomes to those receiving standard intensive chemotherapy. The low-intensity approach resulted in fewer grade ≥3 nonhematologic toxicities, faster hematologic recovery, substantially reduced transfusion needs, and lower overall induction costs. These findings support the LDC regimen as an effective and less toxic alternative for remission induction in pediatric AML.
